{"self_assessment": "Impact: I chose the animal and the design. A big fish was a good fit because its outline reads as a fish with no extra detail. I sketched it on the pad, with the start at the nose, one line over the top and one under the belly, and a forked tail. I laid the whole top line (stroke 1), which every other stretch depended on to get the fall. I also rounded the nose turn into the belly. Before the push, about 123 of the 125 standing dominoes were connected to the start.

Execution: I worked carefully on the fiddly parts. I laid the top line from the start round the head to the nose. I bridged the upper tail onto the top line and nudged the dominoes at the join into line. I inspected the nose, the bridge and the upper-tail join several times to confirm they were dark from the start, since a single joint can stop the whole chain. When everything was connected, I stopped and kept my hands off so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration: I gave clear assignments. Maya took the belly, Priya the tail, and Tom the joints and support, and I kept the pad sketch current so everyone built from the same shape. I asked people to keep clear of spots I was working on, to avoid knocking dominoes over. I also reported on what I checked so the table knew the state of the fish.

Leadership: I set the plan in the first seconds and kept the table on one design. I sequenced the work so the top line went first, the belly followed, and the tail joined last. I redirected people to where they were most useful, then called hands-off once the fish was fully connected. I believe my share of the result is around 40 percent.", "my_share_percent": 40}
